description: Sanhaja Berber confederation from the western Sahara that intervened in Iberia (1086) at the invitation of taifa kings threatened by Alfonso VI of Castile; reunited fragmented taifas under austere Maliki rule and checked Christian expansion for half a century before internal decay and Almohad succession.

lifecycle_phases.description: Taifa kings invite Almoravids from Morocco after Alfonso VI captures Toledo (1085). Yusuf ibn Tashfin defeats Alfonso VI at Sagrajas (1086), halting Christian expansion. Almoravids then conquer the taifa kingdoms themselves, replacing fragmented rule with unified Berber government.

Almoravid empire spans Morocco to Iberia to West African gold fields but cannot hold all fronts simultaneously. Christian reconquest resumes under Alfonso I of Aragon; Lisbon raided. Internal religious reformers (future Almohads) challenge Almoravid legitimacy in Morocco.

rise_factors.description: Almoravid camel-mounted and shock infantry tactics, combined with North African reinforcements, reversed the Christian military advantage; Sagrajas (1086) proved Berber armies superior to Iberian Christian cavalry in pitched battle

Almoravids offered religious orthodoxy (Maliki jurisprudence) and jihad against Christian expansion, giving fragmented taifa Muslims a unifying Islamic identity they had lost under competing petty kings

The Almoravid movement began as a Maliki Islamic reform among Sanhaja Berbers of the Sahara. Rigid adherence to orthodox Sunni practice gave the movement a disciplined, motivated core that regular Iberian Muslim armies lacked.

The Battle of Sagrajas (1086) routed Alfonso VI's Castilian army, rescuing Iberian Muslim taifa kingdoms from imminent collapse and demonstrating that organized Berber infantry could defeat Iberian heavy cavalry.

Almoravid heartlands in the western Sahara controlled trans-Saharan gold trade routes. Gold from Mali/Ghana reached Iberia and Europe via Almoravid merchants, funding military expansion and urban development.

decline_factors.description: Maintaining simultaneous campaigns in Iberia, Morocco, and the Saharan trade routes overstretched Almoravid military and administrative resources; the Strait of Gibraltar crossing created perpetual logistical vulnerability

Almohad religious reform movement arose in Morocco (1120s) and challenged Almoravid legitimacy; by 1147 the Almohads had conquered all of Morocco, leaving the Iberian Almoravids isolated from their base

Iberian Muslims resented Almoravid severity: banning music, burning philosophic texts, and imposing Saharan practices. Urban Al-Andalus educated classes actively collaborated with the Almohad replacement.

The Almohad movement defeated the Almoravids first in Morocco (1147), cutting their supply lines, before completing the conquest of Iberia. The Almoravids faced a two-front war against both Christians and Almohad Berbers.

The Almohad reformers condemned the Almoravids as theologically insufficiently rigorous; their military campaigns from North Africa swept the Almoravid emirs out of Iberia between 1147 and 1172 with the support of Andalusi religious scholars.
